source.title: AL2: Progressive Activation Loss for Learning General Representations in Classification Neural Networks
source.authors: Majed El Helou; F. Dümbgen; S. Süsstrunk

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; supplementary material is referenced but not included.
record.tranche_reason: The study runs label-randomization experiments to assess memorization under regularization, but tests 75% corrupt labels rather than completely random labels.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports MNIST results with 75% corrupt labels. The paper says results for other corruption percentages and datasets are in supplementary material, which is not supplied. Cumulative ablation results are reported separately and do not measure any listed claim version.
record.test_reason: The study reports memorization under conventional regularizers with 75% symmetric label corruption, bearing on V5. Its training trajectories also bear on V6. It does not test V1's completely random labeling condition.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that progressive activation regularization improves learned representations and generalization, assessed using label randomization and cumulative ablation, and combines with batch normalization, dropout, and weight decay.
record.recipe_differences: Uses label randomization to assess memorization as in the cited work, while comparing regularizers and adding progressively increasing activation loss; reported main results use 75% symmetric label corruption.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with regularizer and whether AL2 is used; dropout without AL2 has higher test accuracy and nonzero training loss at epoch 700, while the other unregularized configurations have near-zero loss.

fits_no_version.finding: AL2 increases final test accuracy while retaining high training cross-entropy across all four configurations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Progressively penalizing feature activations reduces memorization and improves generalization under partial label corruption.

fits_no_version.finding: Batch normalization without AL2 reaches training cross-entropy 0.01 under 75% corruption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch normalization does not prevent fitting heavily corrupted training labels in this CNN.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing
record.problems: The supplied main results cover MNIST at 75% corrupt labels only; other datasets and corruption rates are relegated to unavailable supplementary material. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 values at epochs 100–600 are omitted; epoch 700 rows were retained to report final training losses and test accuracies for each configuration. Table 2 cumulative-ablation results are omitted because they do not measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, chance test performance under that labeling, and fitting without changing architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training-time ratios between true and random labels and convergence across corruption fractions.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across corruption fractions from zero to complete corruption; the supplied numerical results cover only 75%.
Completely random labels, data augmentation, and generalization on true labels after removing regularizers. Dropout's final training classification error is not reported.
Separate learning curves for correctly labeled and corrupted examples, and a direct true-label versus fully random-label comparison.

missing.what: Rows capturing temporal evidence for V6. Bare CNN test accuracy falls from 84.20% at epoch 100 to 25.84% at epoch 700 as loss falls from 2.15 to 0.00. Dropout retains approximately 96% test accuracy through epoch 300 before declining to 55.39%, while loss falls from 2.22 to 1.79. These trajectories are declared omitted in rows_left_out but are needed to represent the V6 test.

record.verdict_notes: Corrupted labels are sampled uniformly from incorrect classes, leaving 25% correct labels; this differs from independent random labeling. The supplementary results and training details are unavailable in the supplied text. Nonzero cross-entropy alone does not demonstrate nonzero classification error. The V6 evidence is indirect because clean and corrupted examples are not tracked separately.

versions.untested_parts: The reported experiment uses 75% corrupt labels, not completely random labels; it does not establish test error at chance for completely random labels.
Training time or convergence time for fitting random labels is not compared with fitting true labels.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.
The supplied results do not report training fit and test error across corruption fractions from none to all.
Data augmentation is not tested. The experiments do not establish whether removing regularizers by itself makes generalization on true labels poor.
The study does not measure whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.
